1.pericope_label: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim. From the thirteenth year of Josiah, even unto this day, the word of the Lord hath come unto me, and I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye have not hearkened. They said, Turn ye again now every one from his evil way, and go not after other gods to serve them

schools.summary: Lets both regnal reckonings stand rather than choosing between them, supplies the political setting of the fall of Nineveh and the defeat of Egypt at Carchemish, gives the arithmetic of the twenty-three years and notes that this year apparently saw the first collection of the prophet's utterances; on the chapter's placement it either declines comment or leaves the dispute alone and sets out the structure instead.

Reconciles the dates by the course of events and the principle that a reign shared with a father is justly dated from where it becomes sole, judges the book's order not always chronological, reads the twenty-three years as labour spent without fruit and so a charge of untameable perverseness, presses the mildness of terms that demanded only repentance with a promise of free forgiveness, and grounds the singling out of idolatry in the theocracy, under which protection followed worship.

Explains the conflicting dates by a co-regency, the Jews reckoning from the association and the Chaldeans from the father's death, and holds the chapter utterly out of its place and belonging among the later ones.

Reconciles the dates by overlapping regnal years, makes universal concern the ground of universal cognizance, reads rising early as a heart so set on doing good that it broke the prophet's sleep, and gathers the prophets' message under four heads ending in the rule that we never receive the evil of punishment but where we provoke by the evil of sin.

debates.question: How is the fourth year of Jehoiakim also the first of Nebuchadrezzar, when another account calls it the third?

positions.view: a co-regency: the conqueror was associated with his father two years before his death, so the Jews reckon from the association and the Chaldeans from the death
overlapping regnal years, the one king beginning to reign alone late in his neighbour's third year, while the fourth had opened before the first was complete
an interval filled by events, a father's death calling the conqueror home before he returned to subdue Jehoiakim, with a shared reign justly dated from where it becomes sole
both reckonings may stand together, the setting being the fall of Nineveh and the defeat of Egypt at Carchemish

debates.question: Does the chapter stand where it belongs in the book?

positions.view: utterly out of its place; it should be set among the later chapters
the book is composed of various addresses in which the order of time is not always preserved
notes only that the arrangement carries the reader back to a much earlier period, without a verdict on displacement
leaves the placement question alone and sets out the chapter's structure instead

outliers.reading: Turns rising early into a study of the phrase itself: what men are intent upon they rise early to prosecute, so the words intimate a heart so set on doing good that it broke the prophet's sleep, and morning lectures have their advantages; he adds that many prophets preached sermons never published, and that God keeps account of how long we have enjoyed the means of grace.

Reads the closing clause about their own hurt as mercy rather than threat: nothing can be subtracted from God's rights, so a reproof showing that their rebellion turns only to their own ruin proves that he would not have them perish.

themes: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, that was the first year of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon;
The which Jeremiah the prophet spake unto all the people of Judah, and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying,

From the thirteenth year of Josiah the son of Amon king of Judah, even unto this day, that is the three and twentieth year, the word of the Lord hath come unto me, and I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye have not hearkened.
And the Lord hath sent unto you all his servants the prophets, rising early and sending them; but ye have not hearkened, nor inclined your ear to hear.
They said, Turn ye again now every one from his evil way, and from the evil of your doings, and dwell in the land that the Lord hath given unto you and to your fathers for ever and ever:
And go not after other gods to serve them, and to worship them, and provoke me not to anger with the works of your hands; and I will do you no hurt.
Yet ye have not hearkened unto me, saith the Lord; that ye might provoke me to anger with the works of your hands to your own hurt.

8.pericope_label: Because ye have not heard my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land. Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the candle; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years

schools.summary: Attends to the title given the conqueror and its parallels, corrects the referent of this land and these nations against a wider extension, separates the millstone from the candle as two distinct moments of the domestic day, and reckons the seventy years from the deportation of the king and princes to the decree of return, connecting the figure with the land's unpaid sabbaths and with seventy as a number of completeness.

Hears in the summons the language of a royal edict at whose signal the Chaldeans stand ready, measures the silenced house by degree rather than by routine, since ordinary adversity still leaves marriages and food, notes that the word rendered perpetual is elastic, and declines to date the seventy years at all, taking the term for a correction that softens what had just been called perpetual desolations; the desolation is read as taking in not the city only but all Judea.

Sets the conqueror's service against their refusal to serve in an antithesis, joins the millstone to the candle because the corn was ground before daybreak by candlelight, and counts the seventy years from the fourth year of the reign when the invasion began to the Persian proclamation.

Draws the reciprocity between the messengers of mercy and the messengers of wrath, pairs the instrument of wrath with the instrument of mercy as equally God's servant, supplies the reason within the figure of the darkened house, and calls the starting point of the seventy years a great doubt while inclining to the earlier captivity.

debates.question: In what sense is the conqueror called God's servant?

positions.view: as truly God's servant in wrath as another instrument is in mercy, the man serving God's designs while thinking he served his own

the word is used of David and of Christ, and finds its parallel where another prophet calls the Persian the shepherd and anointed of the Lord, each ruler of the great empires working out purposes he knew nothing of
an antithesis: he shall be God's servant in this work though they would not serve in obeying his commands
the language of a royal edict by which those enlisted assemble, so that the Chaldeans stand under God's power ready at a signal

debates.question: What domestic scene do the millstones and the candle picture?

positions.view: one scene, since the corn was ground before daybreak by candlelight, the mills heard everywhere in the morning and each day's grinding being what that day will consume
two scenes, the millstone the grinding by women for the midday meal and the candle the lamp lit when the day's work is over, so that no words could paint more terribly the breaking up of family life
not the routine but the degree, since ordinary adversity still leaves marriages kept and food prepared, and the loss of all of it marks an extremity beyond common chastisement
the reason lies within the figure: no candle because no work worth candle-light, and no mirth because they have neither cause nor heart for it

debates.question: From what point are the seventy years counted?

positions.view: from the fourth year of the reign, when the invasion began, reaching the Persian king's proclamation exactly
from the deportation of the king and his princes to the decree of return, the figure connected with the land enjoying its denied sabbaths and seventy carrying the sense of completeness
a great doubt between that captivity and a later one eight years after, inclining to the earlier because the nations then began to serve
declines to date it, taking the term for a correction that softens what was just called perpetual desolations and shows the punishment temporary

outliers.reading: Raises two textual points beyond the chronology: that the Hebrew may be rendered a present rather than a future, and that seven manuscripts read and Nebuchadrezzar for and to Nebuchadrezzar, which he calls undoubtedly the true reading.

Corrects the referent of the sentence against a wider extension, insisting that this land means Judah and these nations those around it, rather than the whole compass of peoples named later in the chapter.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts; Because ye have not heard my words,

Behold, I will send and take all the families of the north, saith the Lord, and Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon, my servant, and will bring them against this land, and against the inhabitants thereof, and against all these nations round about, and will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, and an hissing, and perpetual desolations.
Moreover I will take from them the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstones, and the light of the candle.
And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.

12.pericope_label: When seventy years are accomplished, I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have pronounced against it. For many nations and great kings shall serve themselves of them also

schools.summary: Divides over the authenticity of the passage, one voice suspecting interpolation on the evidence of the Greek and of a later veiled prediction and calling the phrase about the book a scribe's addition, the other reporting the critics who pronounce the verses spurious and answering that their main argument is a dogmatic prejudice about what the prophet could have foreseen; both work the closing verb closely, the one correcting an obsolete English idiom and the other reading a prophetic perfect that imposes servitude.

Cares less for the tally than for whom the promise was meant, holding that the time was defined so the faithful might know the covenant was not forgotten and that the words were meant for the elect as food for God's children; presses the idiom of bringing a word as proving its authority by the event, works the closing verb at length against the frigid rendering that they employed them, and draws the conclusion that those who execute God's judgments unconsciously deserve no praise, the proof being the punishment itself.
Supplies its own reckoning of the Babylonian reigns, differing sharply from the other tallies in the years assigned the conqueror, and prefers a genitive pronoun in the phrase rendered that nation.

debates.question: Are these verses the prophet's own?

positions.view: interpolation is likely: the clause naming the king is absent from the Greek, a later verse veils the same prediction in enigmatic language, and the phrase about all that is written in this book is manifestly a scribe's addition
three critics pronounce the verses spurious, but their main argument is a dogmatic prejudice about what the prophet could have foreseen that year

debates.question: How do the seventy years reckon out against the Babylonian regnal lists?

positions.view: through the conqueror's two years with his father and forty-three alone, then the short reigns after, to sixty-nine years and two months, with ten months more to the first year of the Persian
assigns the conqueror thirty-six years where the other reckoning gives forty-five
dates the fall of the city to the allied Medes and Persians, making the interval from the taking of Jerusalem sixty-eight years

debates.question: What does it mean that many nations shall serve themselves of them?

positions.view: the English is a seventeenth-century borrowing from the French and now ambiguous; the sense is to make them their servants

rejects the rendering that they employed them as frigid and ambiguous, since friends may employ one another where the work is mutual, and prefers that they forced them into bondage, the open tense allowing a past of the Babylonians and a future of their subduers
reads the perfect as a prophetic present and glosses the construction as imposing servitude

outliers.reading: Turns the defined term into a doctrine of address rather than of chronology: the words were not spoken indiscriminately to the whole people but meant for the elect, who would have despaired a hundred times without them, a special doctrine given as food for God's children; and to bring a word upon the land is to prove its authority by the event, an expression shaped to men who credit nothing God says until convinced by its accomplishment.
Prefers a textual correction where the others read a tally, holding that the phrase rendered that nation should rather be his nation, the pronoun standing in the genitive.

themes: And it shall come to pass, when seventy years are accomplished, that I will punish the king of Babylon, and that nation, saith the Lord, for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and will make it perpetual desolations.
And I will bring upon that land all my words which I have pronounced against it, even all that is written in this book, which Jeremiah hath prophesied against all the nations.
For many nations and great kings shall serve themselves of them also: and I will recompense them according to their deeds, and according to the works of their own hands.

15.pericope_label: Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. Then took I the cup at the Lord’s hand, and made all the nations to drink: to wit, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof; Pharaoh king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people

schools.summary: Refuses the literal reading of the cup outright, one voice arguing that wrath is no essence to be drunk by a bodily act so that neither cup nor drinking is material, the other calling the supposition a strange example of the literalism of minds incapable of entering into the poetry of a prophet's work; the order of the list is traced in detail from Egypt northwards to Elam and Media and last Babylon, or described as running from south to north, and one transcriber's trace is found in a clause absent from the Greek.

Explains the vision as the writer's own gloss on an oracle that had spoken of all nations abruptly, finding three ends in the telling, and gives two reasons for beginning at Jerusalem, that a father's solicitude is most evident toward his own household and that those taught his will are the less excusable; Egypt follows immediately because it was the fountain of the people's destruction, and the refusal to drink is anticipated and overruled.

Keeps the cup symbolical, one voice taking the taking of it for a public declaration of the tribulation coming and the other saying only that God made the prophet see the appearance of such a cup; the second place in the list is explained politically, this Pharaoh having been the chief instigator of the league against the Chaldeans.

Presses the argument from the house of God outward, that if judgment begins with backsliding professors the wicked need not expect to escape, and insists that the prophet must deliver the word though they will not believe it, since struggling against almighty power is vain.

debates.question: Was there a real cup, and did the prophet carry it to the nations?

positions.view: the question itself results from an imperfect understanding: he receives not a flagon of wine to pass round but a cup filled with the wrath of God, and as wrath is no essence to be drunk by a bodily act the cup is no material cup and the drinking no outward act
a strange example of the literalism of minds incapable of entering into the poetry of a prophet's work
the cup is merely symbolical and the taking of it a public declaration of the tribulation coming
God made him see the appearance of such a cup
he took it in a visionary way

debates.question: Why does the list begin at Jerusalem and pass next to Egypt?

positions.view: a father's solicitude is most evident toward his own household and those taught his will are less excusable; Egypt follows at once because it was the occasion of ruin to the chosen people, who turned their hopes there when they found themselves unequal to Assyria
the prophet passes from the house of God to those without, the order running from south to north

traces the route from Egypt northwards through the Arabian and Philistine borders, then Edom and Moab and Ammon and the Phoenicians, then the desert tribes, then Elam and Media, and last the king of Babylon
the judgment had fallen on Egypt first in fact
this Pharaoh was the chief instigator of the league against the Chaldeans

outliers.reading: Reads the relating of the vision as serving three ends at once, adding authority, testifying that the prophet brought nothing of his own, and showing him a witness against the nations as well as a teacher in the Church; and turns the taking of the cup into a defence of the man who took it, since he was constrained to his office and bound by the divine call, prophets incurring much ill-will as though the calamities they announced were their doing.

Finds a transcriber's trace in the clause as it is this day, absent from the Greek and probably added once the prediction was fulfilled; and makes the reeling of the nations something history has often witnessed, the panic terror of lesser peoples before the march of a great conqueror, their despair and resistance equally infatuated.

themes: For thus saith the Lord God of Israel unto me; Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it.
And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them.
Then took I the cup at the Lord’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, unto whom the Lord had sent me:
To wit, Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and the kings thereof, and the princes thereof, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, an hissing, and a curse; as it is this day;
Pharaoh king of Egypt, and his servants, and his princes, and all his people;

20.pericope_label: And all the mingled people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, and all the kings of the land of the Philistines. Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon, and all the kings of Tyrus and Zidon, and the kings of the isles which are beyond the sea; and all the kingdoms of the world: and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them

schools.summary: Presses the identifications closely: the mingled people are the Ionian and Carian mercenaries settled at Bubastis, the missing Philistine city had dropped out of the confederacy and the remnant phrase belongs to the prophet's own time, the region beyond the sea is a coast-land most probably Cyprus, the utmost corners are those whose temple-corners are shorn, Elam properly means the region of Susa extended by Hebrew writers to all Persia, and the last name is a cypher veiling the true significance at the culminating point of the prophecy.

Supplies from the sense what the history does not give, inferring that the remnant city had been taken but not wholly abandoned because its position was too advantageous, noticing that the three kinsman nations are grouped on purpose, arguing for a plural where the text has a singular island, and pressing the plural kings to show that men of more than one age are summoned; the sequence matters more than the places, since the obscure nation beside the famous ones shows every known part of the earth visited, and the Chaldeans come last because their king was the instrument by whose hand the rest were punished.

Keeps to short identifications, taking the mingled people for strangers settled in Egypt, attributing the fall of the besieged city to one of two named conquerors, preferring the marginal reading that makes the region the Mediterranean sea side with its Phoenician colonies, and reading the last name either as an ancient deified king standing for the city or simply as the king of Babylon, last of all to drink.

debates.question: Who are the mingled people?

positions.view: a mixed population in or near Egypt
strangers settled there

the word is all but identical with the one used of the mixed multitude that left Egypt and of the alien population of Jerusalem, and points to the Ionian and Carian mercenaries settled at Bubastis by the Pharaoh's father

debates.question: What is the region of the isles beyond the sea?

positions.view: the marginal reading is better, the kings of the region by the sea side, the Mediterranean being meant and the Phoenicians having many colonies on its coasts
the Hebrew singular should stand and be rendered a coast-land, wider than our word island, identified probably with Cyprus
the number should be plural, since it is common Hebrew usage to call all countries beyond the sea islands

debates.question: Who is the king of Sheshach, named last?

positions.view: an ancient king of Babylon deified after his death, here standing for either the city or its king
no place of the name is known, so the word is a cypher veiling the true significance, and from its position it is the culminating point of the whole prophecy
simply the king of Babylon, last of all to drink

the order is the point: the Chaldeans come last because their king was the instrument by whose hand the rest were punished, and the Jews were to bear the yoke patiently rather than hasten after his punishment

outliers.reading: Declines the genealogical exercise altogether with a confession worth recording, that these countries are not known in his day, that their extent cannot be learned from geographers, and that hardly a place had failed to change its name long before heathen writers began their records.

Explains why the traders appear in a list of kings, their caravans carrying the commerce between Tyre and Arabia, and corrects the utmost corners from the margin to those who have the corners of their temples shorn, pointing to the nomads of Kedar.

themes: And all the mingled people, and all the kings of the land of Uz, and all the kings of the land of the Philistines, and Ashkelon, and Azzah, and Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod,
Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon,
And all the kings of Tyrus, and all the kings of Zidon, and the kings of the isles which are beyond the sea,
Dedan, and Tema, and Buz, and all that are in the utmost corners,
And all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the mingled people that dwell in the desert,
And all the kings of Zimri, and all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes,
And all the kings of the north, far and near, one with another, and all the kingdoms of the world, which are upon the face of the earth: and the king of Sheshach shall drink after them.

27.pericope_label: Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you. And if they refuse to take the cup at thine hand to drink, then shalt thou say, Ye shall certainly drink. For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name

schools.summary: Defends the offensive word precisely because it offends, as most alien to modern feeling and significant for that reason, implying that the spoilers of Israel should themselves be spoiled and made to disgorge their prey, and reads the image as a terror that makes joint action impossible; the construction of the refusal is given briefly as drinking, ye shall drink, the practical consequence drawn that the nations' safe course was to submit, and the thought of the closing argument recognised as the apostle's, that judgment begins at the house of God.

Uses the repetition to fix what kind of speech this is, since the prophet never carried the message round and the benefit of the predictions belonged only to the Jews, he being introduced as God's herald so that his words might carry greater authority with those who did hear them; the refusal is introduced only to make the answer more striking, and the argument from the less to the greater is put in the figure of the green tree and the dry, with a closing doctrine that the sword is not called forth by the will of man.

Complains of the translators rather than the text, asking why a less offensive word of the same signification was not used, and keeps the historical edge, since the judgment had not merely been threatened but already begun that very year.

debates.question: Should the coarse word have been rendered so?

positions.view: a less offensive word of the same signification might have been used

the word is right precisely because it offends, being most alien to modern feeling and significant for that reason, and implying that the spoilers of Israel should themselves be made to disgorge their prey

debates.question: To whom was this address actually delivered?

positions.view: not to the nations at all: the prophet never carried the message round, neither Tyrians nor Sidonians ever knew their plundering was God's hand at work, and he is introduced as God's herald so that his predictions might carry greater authority with his own people
at face value, as spoken to the several nations already named
spoken so that the nations might learn their wise and safe course, like Judah's, was to accept the punishment and submit

debates.question: What is the refusal to take the cup?

positions.view: a rhetorical device, the refusal introduced to make the answer more striking, men being like unruly horses that kick and rage against the rider
not a refusal to lift a cup but a refusal to credit the prophecies, saying that these things shall not be
a matter of construction, the two verbs giving drinking, ye shall drink
sets the verses out together and carries the sense forward into the roar from on high that follows

outliers.reading: Puts the argument from the less to the greater in his own figure, asking how God should spare aliens to whom he never made any promise if he does not spare the city in which he chose a temple and appointed his name to be invoked, and how the dry can remain safe if the green tree is consumed; and closes on the doctrine that it lies in God's power to excite wars and to quell them, so that the sword, though wielded by the hand of man, is called forth by a hidden power.

Keeps the historical edge on the beginning of judgment, since the evil had not merely been threatened but already begun, that very year bringing the siege and the carrying off of captives, the city being given up to destruction first.

themes: Therefore thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Drink ye, and be drunken, and spue, and fall, and rise no more, because of the sword which I will send among you.
And it shall be, if they refuse to take the cup at thine hand to drink, then shalt thou say unto them, Thus saith the Lord of hosts; Ye shall certainly drink.

For, lo, I begin to bring evil on the city which is called by my name, and should ye be utterly unpunished? Ye shall not be unpunished: for I will call for a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, saith the Lord of hosts.

30.pericope_label: The Lord shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth. For the Lord hath a controversy with the nations. Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind shall be raised up

schools.summary: Complains that one English word does duty for two Hebrew words of very different meaning, God's own dwelling and the pasture of the flock, and finds the shout borrowed from an earlier prophet, the cry of men treading the winepress serving as the war-cry of the Lord of hosts; the controversy is read as a term of law denoting a legal process followed by the technical word for pleading, or the noise taken for the din of war, and the evil that goes from nation to nation is a storm rising on the horizon and spreading over all lands.

Works the same words differently, preferring a loud noise where others hear mournful singing and asking against whom the roaring is directed, then answering that God would come forth conqueror though all combined to extinguish his vengeance; the spreading evil is read as a contagion catching like a distemper or traced instead to God acting by himself, and the slain are called the Lord's because attention is fixed on God alone, who would not be satisfied with three or four nations but shows himself judge of all countries.

Keeps the compass narrow throughout, taking the evil that goes from nation to nation for one people after another falling before the Chaldeans, and reading the slain from one end of the land to the other, so that the desolation described is Palestine's.

Turns the geography into a reproach, since the neighbouring nations might have come to the temple for the knowledge of God and had reason to bless him for their nearness to it, and instead took every opportunity to debauch or disturb the holy city; and closes on the pity of it, that the tender share the common calamity and even those who provoked nobody do not escape.

debates.question: How does the evil travel from nation to nation?

positions.view: as a contagion, catching like a distemper or a fire that consumes one house and then the next, traced through the succession of empires to the Romans
one nation after another falling before the Chaldeans
as a storm rising on the horizon and spreading over the nations, the word being the generic one for a tempest
grants that the nations destroying one another may be admitted, then rejects it: the prophet declares that God's wrath would spread like a storm over all lands

debates.question: How far do the slain of the Lord reach?

positions.view: over all countries, since the prophet sets before us not the ministers of vengeance but God acting by himself, who would not be satisfied with three or four nations
from one end of the earth to the other, the corpses lying unmourned, ungathered and unburied
from one end of the land to the other, the desolation being Palestine's

outliers.reading: Makes the sharpest complaint against the English in the chapter, that one word does duty for two Hebrew words of very different meaning, the first God's own dwelling from which the thunder of his wrath is heard and the second the pasture of the flock on whom the storm falls, an association that may turn the roaring into that of a lion attacking the flock; and reads the controversy as a legal process rather than a debate, so that God appears as Accuser in a suit where he is also the supreme Judge.

Raises and answers the objection he expects at the sudden commotion, what it can mean that God should raise one after lying quiet for ages, replying that the time of contending is not always and that one who forbears to bring his adversary at once before the judge is dealing kindly with him meanwhile.

themes: Therefore prophesy thou against them all these words, and say unto them, The Lord shall roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation; he shall mightily roar upon his habitation; he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.
A noise shall come even to the ends of the earth; for the Lord hath a controversy with the nations, he will plead with all flesh; he will give them that are wicked to the sword, saith the Lord.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth.

And the slain of the Lord shall be at that day from one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth: they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried; they shall be dung upon the ground.

34.pericope_label: Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter are accomplished. And the shepherds shall have no way to flee. He hath forsaken his covert, as the lion: for their land is desolate because of the fierceness of the oppressor

schools.summary: Reads the shepherds as rulers, the principal of the flock being the best and fattest of the rams and standing for the princes and captains, with no rank spared, and objects twice to what the translators supplied, the added words at the wallowing leaving an unauthorised interpretation and the insertion at the cry reducing the dramatic vividness of the Hebrew to the tamest prose; the lion leaving his covert is God, the thunder of whose wrath is the roar, and the closing word is canvassed at length before the English is left standing.

Dissents from the common reading of the shepherds, holding that the prophet turns here especially to his own nation, a thing interpreters have not observed and for want of observing have not understood his meaning, so that the passage returns from the nations to the Jews; measures the denial of flight as a loss beyond exile, finds the adjective in peaceable habitations deliberate against those who inferred future safety from past quiet, and fixes what God forsakes as his own Temple and city.

Takes the shepherds for kings and chiefs and reaches for the figure of a precious vessel of crystal or agate which a fall shatters beyond mending, and states the plain effect of the last verse, that the rising up of God out of his covert leaves the land desolate through the fierceness of the enemy, caused by the fierce anger of God; the lion itself is kept as an animal driven from the river banks when they overflow.

debates.question: Who are the shepherds summoned to howl?

positions.view: kings and chiefs
the principal of the flock are the best and fattest of the rams, standing for the princes and captains
rulers of every rank, none being spared
the prophet turns here especially to his own nation, a thing interpreters have not observed, so that the passage returns from the nations to the Jews

debates.question: Who forsakes his covert as the lion?

positions.view: God, the thunder of whose wrath is the lion's roar, going forth from his hiding-place to the work of vengeance
God, but the point is what he forsakes, his own Temple and city, against a people who had made a proverb of the saying that this was his rest for ever
reports the reading that God leaves the temple but allows equally that the conqueror may be meant, leaving Babylon his den and ranging for prey
the animal itself, the lion driven from the river banks when they overflow and coming with ravening fierceness into open country

outliers.reading: Closes the chapter on a single word, noting that the term for the oppressor's fierceness may by a slight change be read as the sword of oppression, that the same word also means dove and was so taken by the Latin, the bird having been blazoned, it is said, on the Babylonian standards and become a symbol of their power, and yet concluding after all of it that there is no reason to alter the English.

Finds the adjective in peaceable habitations deliberate, since the Jews inferred future safety from enemies not having disturbed them before; and while the faithful rightly argue from past kindness that God will be kind still, hypocrites who never repent absurdly conclude that he is bound to them and go on securely while daily provoking him.

themes: Howl, ye shepherds, and cry; and wallow yourselves in the ashes, ye principal of the flock: for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished; and ye shall fall like a pleasant vessel.
And the shepherds shall have no way to flee, nor the principal of the flock to escape.
A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and an howling of the principal of the flock, shall be heard: for the Lord hath spoiled their pasture.
And the peaceable habitations are cut down because of the fierce anger of the Lord.
He hath forsaken his covert, as the lion: for their land is desolate because of the fierceness of the oppressor, and because of his fierce anger.
